CLOUD SECURITY WITH AWS IAM

By
Emmanuel Aidoo
September 2026

Introducing Today's Project!

Project overview

In this project, I will demonstrate how to launch EC2 instances, apply custom
resource tags, and restrict user permissions using JSON-based IAM policies. I'm
doing this project to learn cloud access control best practices and how to safely
onboard team members with environment-speciﬁc permissions.

Tools and concepts

The key services and concepts I learned in this project include launching Amazon
EC2 virtual instances, using Environment Tags to organize resources, writing
custom JSON-based IAM Policies to enforce granular access control, conﬁguring
an Account Alias for friendly sign-in URLs, and managing user permissions
securely through IAM Users and User Groups.

Project reflection

This project took me approximately 1 hour to complete. The most challenging part
was carefully reviewing and applying the JSON policy structure with environment
tags, while it was most rewarding to successfully test the intern IAM user and
watch the console correctly block production actions while allowing full access to
the development instance.

Tags

What I did in this step

In this step, I will launch two Amazon EC2 instances (one for production and one
for development) because we need to increase NextWork's computing power to
handle increased holiday website traffic and properly segment our environments
for testing.

Understanding tags

Tags are like custom labels or metadata attached to AWS resources that help
organize, ﬁlter, and identify them. They are useful because they allow us to easily
group resources by environment (such as production versus development), track
costs, and apply resource-level IAM policies based on speciﬁc tag values.

My tag configuration

The tag I’ve used on my EC2 instances is called Env. The values I’ve assigned for
my instances are production for the production server and development for the
development server.

IAM Policies

What I did in this step

In this step, I will create a custom JSON-based IAM policy called
NextWorkDevEnvironmentPolicy because we need to grant our new intern
granular permissions to manage the development EC2 instance while explicitly
restricting them from touching the production environment.

Understanding IAM policies

IAM policies are rules and permissions assigned to users, groups, or roles that
explicitly state what actions are allowed or denied on speciﬁc AWS resources,
and under what conditions those rules apply.

The policy I set up

For this project, I’ve set up a policy using JSON because it allows for precise,
granular control over resource tags (like restricting access to development
environments) that can be quickly pasted and conﬁgured directly in the AWS
console.

Policy effect

I’ve created a policy that allows all EC2 actions (ec2:*) speciﬁcally for resources
tagged with Env = development, while permitting general ec2:Describe* actions
and explicitly denying permission to create or delete tags (ec2:DeleteTags,
ec2:CreateTags). This ensures interns can manage development servers without
altering environment tags or touching production resources.

Understanding Effect, Action, and Resource

The Effect, Action, and Resource attributes of a JSON policy deﬁne the core
permission rules: Effect determines whether the statement allows or denies
access (such as Allow or Deny), Action speciﬁes exactly what operations are
permitted or blocked (such as ec2:*), and Resource identiﬁes which speciﬁc AWS
targets or services the rule applies to (such as * for all resources)

Account Alias

What I did in this step

In this step, I will create an AWS account alias because it provides a friendly,
customized URL for our account (such as our team name instead of a long string
of digits), making it much easier and more professional for our new intern to ﬁnd
and log into the AWS Management Console.

Understanding account aliases

An account alias is a unique, user-friendly name you create to replace your 12-
digit AWS account ID in your sign-in URL, making it much easier and more
professional for team members and interns to remember and access the AWS
Management Console.

IAM Users and User Groups

What I did in this step

In this step, I will create a dedicated IAM user group and user for our new intern
because it allows us to manage permissions centrally and securely grant them
access to the management console without exposing production resources.

Understanding user groups

IAM user groups are collections of IAM users that allow you to manage
permissions for multiple users at once by attaching policies directly to the group
rather than managing each user individually.

Attaching policies to user groups

I attached the policy I created to this user group, which means all users placed
inside this group automatically inherit those exact permissions—granting them
full access to manage development-tagged EC2 instances while blocking them
from touching production resources or managing resource tags.

Understanding IAM users

IAM users are individual identities created within AWS that represent people or
services needing access to the account, each equipped with their own unique
security credentials like passwords or access keys.

Logging in as an IAM User

Sharing sign-in details

The ﬁrst way is to copy and download the .csv ﬁle containing the user's security
credentials and sign-in link, which can then be securely shared with them. The
second way is to directly copy the autogenerated console password and sign-in
URL from the AWS console and send them to the user via a secure
communication channel.

Observations from the IAM user dashboard

Once I logged in as my IAM user, I noticed that several dashboard panels
displayed an Access Denied message. This was because the user account is
restricted by a custom IAM policy that limits permissions exclusively to the
development environment and blocks broad visibility across unauthorized
resources.

Testing IAM Policies

What I did in this step

In this step, I will log into the AWS console using the new intern's IAM user
credentials and test their access because we need to verify that our custom IAM
policy successfully grants them permission to manage the development EC2
instance while correctly blocking them from modifying the production
environment.

Testing policy actions

I tested my JSON IAM policy by attempting to stop both the production and
development EC2 instances as the new intern user; the console successfully
blocked me from stopping the production instance with an authorization error,
while allowing me to manage and interact with the development instance as
permitted by our environment tag rules.

Stopping the production instance

When I tried to stop the production instance, an error message popped up at the
top of the console stating that I was not authorized to perform that action. This
was because the IAM policy correctly blocked my user account from modifying
or stopping any resources tagged with the production environment.

Stopping the development instance

When I tried to stop the development instance, the operation succeeded without
any errors. This conﬁrmed that our custom IAM policy successfully granted my
user account full permissions to manage and modify EC2 instances tagged with
the development environment.

IAM Policy Simulator

In this secret mission, I am exploring how to use the IAM Policy Simulator to test
user permissions safely without affecting real AWS resources, and I'm doing this
because shutting down live development or production instances can be
disruptive to other engineers and users during testing.

Understanding the IAM Policy Simulator

The IAM Policy Simulator is useful because it allows you to safely test and
troubleshoot complex permission policies and simulate user actions without
risking any accidental changes, deletions, or disruptions to live production
resources.

How I used the simulator

When I ran the simulation for the development instance, the results showed an
Allowed status for actions like starting, stopping, and describing the instance,
conﬁrming that our custom IAM policy successfully granted the intern full
management permissions over resources tagged with the development
environment.
